explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The LORD tells Moses to say, "…if a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD…" (Numbers 6:2). Nobody needs a title, a tribe or a fancy hat for this one. I own a very tall hat and it still doesn't count for anything here.

Close, but the text opens the door wider. The LORD says "if a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite…" (Numbers 6:2). Priests aren't mentioned as the only ones who can make it. In fact, a priest shows up later to help with the offerings, not to be the only one making the vow.

Nope, no leader requirement anywhere in the verse. The LORD says "if a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD…" (Numbers 6:2). A man or a woman, that's the whole guest list. Nobody has to be in charge of anything to sign up.

I see the thinking, friend. No wine in grape juice, so what's the problem? But the text says he "must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins" (Numbers 6:3). It's about the grapevine itself, not only the drink. I'll admit I'd have been checking the snack drawer for loopholes too.

Right, it's False. The text says he "must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins" (Numbers 6:3). Then it goes further: nothing from the grapevine at all, not even seeds or skins (Numbers 6:4). The rule isn't just about wine. It covers the whole vine.
That's the one. "…no razor shall touch his head" (Numbers 6:5). He lets the hair of his head grow long for the whole vow. Meanwhile some of us can't go a full week without fiddling with our mustache.

Good guess, since long hair would need some attention. But the text never mentions a comb. It says "no razor shall touch his head" (Numbers 6:5). So the hair grows, and nobody is told to stop brushing it.

A crown is a fun guess, friend, and that's a fancy hat I'd love to try on. But the verse says "no razor shall touch his head" (Numbers 6:5). Nothing about crowns anywhere in the rule. The only head gear in my bakery is a tall white chef's hat, and it's not part of any vow.

I get why that sounds fair, friend. Family is family. But the text says "Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die, he is not to defile himself…" (Numbers 6:7). No exception for even the closest relatives. I think that's a heavy one, and I'm not going to joke about it.

Right, it's False. The text says "Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die, he is not to defile himself…" (Numbers 6:7). It names the closest family on purpose, so there's no "just this once." I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage, and it's good to read it slowly.

explanations.answer: His head carries the sign of his vow to God
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the reason the verse gives. He isn't to defile himself "because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head" (Numbers 6:7). The long hair is that symbol. So the reason is right there on top of him.

explanations.answer: His hands carry the offerings for the altar
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, since offerings show up later in the passage. But the verse gives a different reason. He is not to defile himself "because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head" (Numbers 6:7). It's about his head, not his hands. I'd know about hands, friend. Mine come with a mustache.

explanations.answer: His robe carries the mark of his tribe
explanations.explanation: Interesting idea, but the text never mentions a robe or a tribal mark here. The reason is "because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head" (Numbers 6:7). So the sign is on his head. That's where the whole rule points.

That's it, friend. If someone suddenly dies in his presence and defiles his consecrated hair, "he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing—the seventh day" (Numbers 6:9). The hair was the symbol, so it's the hair that goes. Rough day, I think, and a very breezy one.

Washing clothes is a fair guess, since cleansing sounds like laundry. But this passage says something else. "…he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing—the seventh day" (Numbers 6:9). The head is the focus here, not the wardrobe.

I can see why, friend. Oil on the head sounds like a big ceremony. But the text says "he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing—the seventh day" (Numbers 6:9). No oil mentioned for this step. The hair comes off instead.

Yes, the seventh. The text says he "must shave his head on the day of his cleansing—the seventh day" (Numbers 6:9). Then the eighth day brings the offerings (Numbers 6:10). Seven days is a long time to wait with a defiled head.

Not the third, friend. The text says the day of cleansing is "the seventh day" (Numbers 6:9). The third day isn't mentioned anywhere in this part. The count goes all the way to seven before the head is shaved.

Ten is a nice round number, but the text doesn't use it. The day of cleansing is "the seventh day" (Numbers 6:9). The offerings come the day after, on the eighth (Numbers 6:10). So the tenth day isn't part of this one.

That's right. After the sin offering and the burnt offering, the text says "On that day he must consecrate his head again" (Numbers 6:11). The priest offers them "to make atonement for him" (Numbers 6:11). So the head gets set apart to the LORD once more.

It's actually True, friend. After the two birds are offered, the text says "On that day he must consecrate his head again" (Numbers 6:11). So he doesn't just walk away from the offerings. The head is set apart again, right then.

Ouch, but yes. The text says "…the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled" (Numbers 6:12). He rededicates his time of separation and starts over. I think that's a tough one, like losing a whole batch to a dropped tray.

explanations.answer: They count toward the new vow
explanations.explanation: I wish, friend. But the text says "…the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled" (Numbers 6:12). He rededicates his time of separation and brings a year-old male lamb as a guilt offering. The days he already kept don't carry over.

Half credit would be generous, but the text doesn't say that. It says "…the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled" (Numbers 6:12). None of them count. The new time of separation starts fresh.

That's right. The Nazirite is "to shave his consecrated head, take the hair, and put it on the fire under the peace offering" (Numbers 6:18). So the long hair ends up on the fire, under the offering. After all that growing, that's quite the finish.

The basket is in this passage, but it holds something else. It's the "basket of unleavened cakes" (Numbers 6:15). The hair goes "on the fire under the peace offering" (Numbers 6:18). So the basket is for the bread, not the hair.

Good thought, since that's where hair usually lands. But the text says he is to "take the hair, and put it on the fire under the peace offering" (Numbers 6:18). It doesn't go on the ground. It goes into the fire.

Yes, the priest. After the wave offering, the text says "This is a holy portion for the priest, in addition to the breast of the wave offering and the thigh that was presented" (Numbers 6:20). So the priest gets the shoulder, the cake and the wafer, plus those extras. Not a bad payday for the one doing all that waving.

I see why, since they were put into his hands first (Numbers 6:19). But after the priest waves them, the text says "This is a holy portion for the priest…" (Numbers 6:20). So they end up as the priest's portion. The Nazirite just holds them for a moment.

Levites are a fair guess, friend, since they worked around the Tent too. But this verse names someone else. "This is a holy portion for the priest…" (Numbers 6:20). The Levites aren't mentioned in this part of the passage.

That's right. The text ends the whole thing with "After that, the Nazirite may drink wine" (Numbers 6:20). The shave and the wave offering come first, then the vow is done. After all those days of grape rules, I bet that's a big moment.
It's actually True, friend. After the shave and the wave offering, the text says "After that, the Nazirite may drink wine" (Numbers 6:20). So the grape rules don't last forever. The vow has an end.

That's it, friend. The text says "…he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation" (Numbers 6:21). No shortcuts, no trading it in. A promise like this one gets finished.

Tempting, I know. Some of us shorten a diet by lunchtime. But the text says "…he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation" (Numbers 6:21). Nothing about cutting it short. He sees it through.

A priest does help with the offerings, but the vow isn't handed off. The text says "…he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation" (Numbers 6:21). The one who made it is the one who fulfills it.
